105	\section{Controlled Evaluation Subset}
106	\label{sec:fair_subset}
107	
108	The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential output quality: the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) at the \texttt{max\_new\_tokens} limit, versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To control for this, we define a \emph{controlled evaluation subset} that excludes any document where either model produces a truncated or repetitive output. An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the canonical (s42) evidence tax is +6.2pp (vs.\ +8.04pp on the full set for s42; multi-seed mean tax is +4.82pp), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the s42 gap. The positive direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.
109	
110	Table~\ref{tab:mechanistic} provides a mechanistic breakdown across three scales. Output duplication rate (fraction of documents containing $\geq$3 repeated triples or unique/total $< 0.5$) declines monotonically with scale for both training configurations, but the gap between no-evidence and with-evidence models narrows from 27.5pp at 1.7B to 3.7pp at 8B. This pattern supports the implicit regularization hypothesis: evidence generation forces smaller models to attend to supporting context, reducing degenerate repetition. At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so the regularization benefit diminishes, while the model lacks sufficient capacity to jointly optimize extraction and evidence generation, creating the capacity valley that produces the largest evidence tax ($-3.63$pp, three-seed SFT mean). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.
111

22	
23	Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the primary comparison on Qwen3-4B. The SFT baseline exhibits high seed sensitivity: three-seed mean Ign-F1 is 43.58 with standard deviation 3.80pp (individual seeds range from 39.74 to 47.34). This variance is comparable to the evidence tax itself ($-3.63$ points), indicating that single-seed evaluation can substantially misestimate the true cost of joint evidence generation. Removing evidence entirely (no-evidence SFT) reaches 47.21 Ign-F1.
24	
25	RSFT CED achieves a three-seed mean of 44.82 Ign-F1 (+1.24 over SFT mean). RSFT training from a fixed SFT checkpoint is highly reproducible (std 0.51pp across three seeds), contrasting with the large cross-seed SFT variance (std 3.80pp), though these reflect different sources of variation (Section~\ref{sec:scaling}). Even the weakest RSFT seed (44.23) exceeds the SFT mean (43.58), and every RSFT seed outperforms two of three SFT seeds. Evidence quality improves (Evi-F1 80.96 vs.\ 79.61) and coupling tightens (EDCR 0.6487 vs.\ 0.6797). CED-based selection thus provides two complementary benefits: it raises mean extraction performance and stabilizes it across training runs. Per-seed results appear in Appendix~\ref{sec:ablation_full}.
26	
27	The remaining gap to the no-evidence upper bound (2.39 points) represents the residual cost of producing structured evidence, a cost that varies with model scale (Section~\ref{sec:scaling}).

lines: The evidence tax, defined as the Ign-F1 difference between no-evidence and joint-evidence SFT, varies across model scales and training seeds. Table~\ref{tab:scaling} presents multi-seed results across four models (Figure~\ref{fig:scaling} in Appendix).

-A key finding from multi-seed evaluation is that the apparent magnitude of the evidence tax is sensitive to SFT seed variance. At 4B, the three-seed tax is $-3.63$ points, but individual seeds range from $-0$ (s44) to $-7.47$ (s42). The SFT standard deviation of 3.80pp is comparable to the tax itself, meaning single-seed evaluation can substantially overestimate or underestimate the true cost. At 8B, the two-seed mean tax is $-2.13$ (Qwen3-8B) and $-0.68$ for LLaMA-3.1-8B. The most surprising result appears at 1.7B: instead of paying a larger tax, the smallest model \emph{benefits} from evidence generation (+4.82 points, three-seed mean). Individual seeds vary substantially (s42: +8.04, s43: +3.04, s44: +3.39), but all three consistently benefit. The no-evidence model suffers a higher truncation rate, partially inflating the gap; a controlled evaluation on the canonical seed (Appendix~\ref{sec:fair_subset}) confirms the benefit is genuine. We hypothesize that evidence generation provides implicit regularization for small models, forcing attention to supporting context rather than surface-level memorization.

+Table~\ref{tab:scaling} reports evidence taxes from s42 paired comparisons (the only seed with no-evidence evaluation). The tax is non-monotonic with scale: evidence generation \emph{helps} at 1.7B (+8.04pp), substantially hurts at 4B ($-7.47$pp), and is near-neutral at 8B ($-0.28$pp for Qwen3, $-0.68$pp for LLaMA). These are single-seed estimates, and the 4B tax may be inflated because s42 is the weakest SFT seed at that scale (39.74 Ign-F1 vs.\ 43.65 and 47.34 for s43 and s44); multi-seed no-evidence evaluation is needed for reliable tax estimates. The 1.7B benefit is partially inflated by differential truncation rates; a controlled evaluation (Appendix~\ref{sec:fair_subset}) confirms a genuine benefit of +6.2pp on a fair subset. We hypothesize that evidence generation provides implicit regularization for small models, forcing attention to supporting context rather than surface-level memorization.

RSFT improves mean performance at all scales: +6.55 for 1.7B, +1.24 for 4B, and +5.48 for 8B. RSFT training from a shared SFT checkpoint is also highly reproducible: three seeds yield std 0.09pp at 1.7B ($n{=}3$), 0.51pp at 4B ($n{=}3$), and 0.53pp at 8B ($n{=}2$). While SFT models show substantially larger cross-seed variation (std 2.79pp at 1.7B, 3.80pp at 4B, 2.62pp at 8B), these two sources of variance are not directly comparable: SFT variance reflects full training runs from different random seeds, whereas RSFT variance reflects only the additional fine-tuning stage from a fixed SFT base. RSFT lifts the weakest SFT seed most: the 4B s42 SFT (39.74 Ign-F1) produces RSFT seeds ranging 44.16--45.12, recovering over 4pp that SFT variability lost. At 8B, the RSFT gain is +5.48 rather than the +3.73 observed in single-seed comparison, because multi-seed SFT averaging exposes higher baseline instability. Every 1.7B RSFT seed outperforms every observed 8B SFT seed (+0.58pp minimum gap), suggesting that a 4.7$\times$ smaller model can match or exceed 8B-level performance with RSFT applied to evidence-grounded extraction.

lines: \section{Controlled Evaluation Subset}
\label{sec:fair_subset}

-The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential output quality: the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) at the \texttt{max\_new\_tokens} limit, versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To control for this, we define a \emph{controlled evaluation subset} that excludes any document where either model produces a truncated or repetitive output. An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the canonical (s42) evidence tax is +6.2pp (vs.\ +8.04pp on the full set for s42; multi-seed mean tax is +4.82pp), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the s42 gap. The positive direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.

+The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential output quality: the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) at the \texttt{max\_new\_tokens} limit, versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To control for this, we define a \emph{controlled evaluation subset} that excludes any document where either model produces a truncated or repetitive output. An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the s42 evidence tax is +6.2pp (vs.\ +8.04pp on the full set), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the gap. The positive direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.

Table~\ref{tab:mechanistic} provides a mechanistic breakdown across three scales. Output duplication rate (fraction of documents containing $\geq$3 repeated triples or unique/total $< 0.5$) declines monotonically with scale for both training configurations, but the gap between no-evidence and with-evidence models narrows from 27.5pp at 1.7B to 3.7pp at 8B. This pattern supports the implicit regularization hypothesis: evidence generation forces smaller models to attend to supporting context, reducing degenerate repetition. At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so the regularization benefit diminishes, while the model lacks sufficient capacity to jointly optimize extraction and evidence generation, creating the capacity valley that produces the largest evidence tax ($-3.63$pp, three-seed SFT mean). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) methods now match or exceed encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet they produce bare relation triplets without identifying the sentences that support each prediction.
In deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems, users cannot verify predictions without manually locating textual evidence across multi-page documents.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) can produce supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy. The community therefore faces a gap between extractive precision and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT).
Our study spans 85+ experimental configurations across four model scales (1.7B to 8B parameters), two model families, and two datasets.
We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic tool and NLI-based scoring for sample selection.

Three findings emerge.
First, RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity: GRPO causes catastrophic decoupling, DPO shows gradual degradation, and RSFT preserves stable joint performance.
Second, the cost of evidence production varies across model scales: at 1.7B parameters evidence provides a +6.2pp Ign-F1 benefit on a controlled evaluation subset excluding truncated and repetitive outputs, at 4B it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty, and at 8B the cost approaches zero.
Third, RSFT with NLI-based scoring is the most effective route: it achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over supervised fine-tuning at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51).

\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
4	Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
5	These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
6	Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
7	In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.
8	
9	The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
10	Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
11	When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
12	Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
13	Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
14	Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
15	However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
16	The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.
17	
18	This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
19	In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
20	The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
21	In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
22	Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
23	Whether this generation cost necessarily harms extraction, or whether the interaction is more nuanced, remains an open question: the answer may depend on model scale and optimization strategy.
24	This uncertainty motivates a systematic investigation of how evidence production interacts with extraction quality across model scales and optimization paradigms.
25	
26	We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
27	Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
28	\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
29	GRPO with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
30	Catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with QLoRA-based GRPO training, though we note that GRPO with full-precision training (bf16, $G{=}8$) achieves EDCR below the SFT baseline, indicating that the decoupling is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
31	\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations varies across model scales.
32	At 1.7B parameters, evidence generation provides an implicit regularization benefit of +6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at 8B, the tax approaches zero.
33	This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
34	\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring for training data selection emerges as the most effective optimization route.
35	By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.
36	
37	Our contributions are as follows:
38	\begin{enumerate}
39	    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs and conduct the first \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across four model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms.
40	
41	    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure is associated with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR), a diagnostic that tracks misalignment between extraction and evidence capabilities, as an analytical tool throughout our study. EDCR shares Rel-Recall with Rel-F1 by construction; we interpret the observed cross-method correlation ($\rho = -0.89$, $n = 7$) as a diagnostic pattern rather than an independent finding, and validate through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$) that avoids the shared-component concern.
42	
43	    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of joint evidence production varies across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, challenging the assumption that evidence generation uniformly degrades extraction quality.
44	
45	    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective solution, using CED or flat-NLI to select high-quality training data. RSFT achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.
46	\end{enumerate}
47

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
Whether this generation cost necessarily harms extraction, or whether the interaction is more nuanced, remains an open question: the answer may depend on model scale and optimization strategy.
This uncertainty motivates a systematic investigation of how evidence production interacts with extraction quality across model scales and optimization paradigms.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
GRPO with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
Catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with QLoRA-based GRPO training, though we note that GRPO with full-precision training (bf16, $G{=}8$) achieves EDCR below the SFT baseline, indicating that the decoupling is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations varies across model scales.
At 1.7B parameters, evidence generation provides an implicit regularization benefit of +6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at 8B, the tax approaches zero.
This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring for training data selection emerges as the most effective optimization route.
By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs and conduct the first \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across four model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure is associated with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR), a diagnostic that tracks misalignment between extraction and evidence capabilities, as an analytical tool throughout our study. EDCR shares Rel-Recall with Rel-F1 by construction; we interpret the observed cross-method correlation ($\rho = -0.89$, $n = 7$) as a diagnostic pattern rather than an independent finding, and validate through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$) that avoids the shared-component concern.

    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of joint evidence production varies across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, challenging the assumption that evidence generation uniformly degrades extraction quality.

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective solution, using CED or flat-NLI to select high-quality training data. RSFT achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
Whether this generation cost necessarily harms extraction, or whether the interaction is more nuanced, remains an open question: the answer may depend on model scale and optimization strategy.
This uncertainty motivates a systematic investigation of how evidence production interacts with extraction quality across model scales and optimization paradigms.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
GRPO with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
Catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with QLoRA-based GRPO training, though we note that GRPO with full-precision training (bf16, $G{=}8$) achieves EDCR below the SFT baseline, indicating that the decoupling is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations varies across model scales.
At 1.7B parameters, evidence generation provides an implicit regularization benefit of +6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at 8B, the tax approaches zero.
This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring for training data selection emerges as the most effective optimization route.
By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs and conduct the first \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across four model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure is associated with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR), a diagnostic that tracks misalignment between extraction and evidence capabilities, as an analytical tool throughout our study. EDCR shares Rel-Recall with Rel-F1 by construction; we interpret the observed cross-method correlation ($\rho = -0.89$, $n = 7$) as a diagnostic pattern rather than an independent finding, and validate through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$) that avoids the shared-component concern.

    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of joint evidence production varies across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, challenging the assumption that evidence generation uniformly degrades extraction quality.

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective solution, using CED or flat-NLI to select high-quality training data. RSFT achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
Whether this generation cost necessarily harms extraction, or whether the interaction is more nuanced, remains an open question: the answer may depend on model scale and optimization strategy.
This uncertainty motivates a systematic investigation of how evidence production interacts with extraction quality across model scales and optimization paradigms.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning five model scales (1.7B to 14B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
GRPO with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
Catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with QLoRA-based GRPO training, though we note that GRPO with full-precision training (bf16, $G{=}8$) achieves EDCR below the SFT baseline, indicating that the decoupling is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations varies across model scales.
At 1.7B parameters, evidence generation provides an implicit regularization benefit of +6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at $\geq$8B, the tax approaches zero.
This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring for training data selection emerges as the most effective optimization route.
By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs and conduct the first \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across five model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure is associated with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR), a diagnostic that tracks misalignment between extraction and evidence capabilities, as an analytical tool throughout our study. EDCR shares Rel-Recall with Rel-F1 by construction; we interpret the observed cross-method correlation ($\rho = -0.89$, $n = 7$) as a diagnostic pattern rather than an independent finding, and validate through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$) that avoids the shared-component concern.

    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of joint evidence production varies across 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters, challenging the assumption that evidence generation uniformly degrades extraction quality.

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective solution, using CED or flat-NLI to select high-quality training data. RSFT achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.
\end{enumerate}

An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the s42 evidence tax is +6.2pp (vs.\ +8.04pp on the full set), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the gap. The positive direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.

At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so the regularization benefit diminishes, while the model lacks sufficient capacity to jointly optimize extraction and evidence generation, creating the capacity valley that produces the largest evidence tax ($-7.47$pp, s42 paired). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.

\section{Full Ablation Results}
\label{sec:ablation_full}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation_full} reports the complete RSFT ablation across scoring functions, top-$k$ values, and random seeds. RSFT CED $k{=}1$ achieves a four-seed mean Ign-F1 of 44.66 (standard deviation 0.49), confirming robust improvement over the SFT s42 baseline (39.74). The three-seed mean reported in Table~\ref{tab:main} (44.82, seeds 42/43/44) is slightly higher because it excludes the lowest seed (s45: 44.16). Random selection RSFT $k{=}1$ (41.14 Ign-F1), which samples from the same candidate pool without CED scoring, improves only +1.40pp over SFT s42 versus +4.92pp for CED RSFT, confirming that CED scoring precision drives the majority of the RSFT gain. Increasing $k$ to 3 slightly degrades performance (43.64 Ign-F1), consistent with the intuition that stricter selection yields higher-quality training data. The flat-NLI scoring variant produces comparable Rel-F1 (mean 45.61 vs.\ 45.63 for CED, a difference of 0.02pp). Both CED and flat-NLI improve substantially over the SFT baseline while maintaining or improving Evi-F1, confirming that the RSFT gains are driven by quality-based data selection rather than by the specific contrastive formulation.

\paragraph{NLI scoring comparison.} Across all available seeds, CED RSFT achieves mean Rel-F1 of 45.63 (seeds 42, 43, 44, 45: range 45.14--46.21), and flat-NLI RSFT achieves mean Rel-F1 of 45.61 (seeds 42, 43: range 45.35--45.86). The 0.02pp difference suggests comparable performance: CED's contrastive design does not substantially outperform simpler NLI scoring for RSFT data selection. We adopt CED as the default because its contrastive formulation produces per-triple discrimination scores that support interpretable error analysis.

\paragraph{Top-$k$ selection.} Best-of-8 ($k{=}1$) yields mean Ign-F1 44.66 and Rel-F1 45.63, while top-3-of-8 ($k{=}3$) produces 43.64 and 44.54. The selected training data confirms the quality gap: $k{=}1$ data has mean extraction F1 of 61.57 and mean CED of 0.6683, versus 57.61 and 0.6205 for $k{=}3$. Despite $k{=}3$ providing 2.96$\times$ more training examples, the additional lower-ranked samples introduce noise that degrades final performance.

\label{sec:scaling_details}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_detail} supplements Table~\ref{tab:scaling} in the main text with per-scale Rel-F1 and Evi-F1 breakdowns. At 1.7B, RSFT improves Rel-F1 from 45.86 to 52.81 (+6.95, multi-seed mean) while achieving Evi-F1 82.63 and EDCR 0.6217. The 4B model shows the same pattern: Rel-F1 increases from 44.39 to 45.80 (+1.41, three-seed mean). \section{Controlled Evaluation Subset}
\label{sec:fair_subset}

The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential output quality: the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) at the \texttt{max\_new\_tokens} limit, versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To control for this, we define a \emph{controlled evaluation subset} that excludes any document where either model produces a truncated or repetitive output. An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the s42 evidence tax is +6.2pp (vs.\ +8.04pp on the full set), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the gap. The positive direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.

Table~\ref{tab:mechanistic} provides a mechanistic breakdown across three scales. Output duplication rate (fraction of documents containing $\geq$3 repeated triples or unique/total $< 0.5$) declines monotonically with scale for both training configurations, but the gap between no-evidence and with-evidence models narrows from 27.5pp at 1.7B to 3.7pp at 8B. This pattern supports the implicit regularization hypothesis: evidence generation forces smaller models to attend to supporting context, reducing degenerate repetition. At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so the regularization benefit diminishes, while the model lacks sufficient capacity to jointly optimize extraction and evidence generation, creating the capacity valley that produces the largest evidence tax ($-7.47$pp, s42 paired). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.
